title: JSON and Structured Data
learningObjectives: Explain the key ideas and terminology of json and structured data.
Recognize how the concept is used in real software communication.
Identify common mistakes or risks associated with this topic.
Apply the concept to a small, fictional API scenario.
Review a communication design and justify appropriate choices.

understand.concept: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for representing structured data. It supports objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. JSON does not directly support comments, functions, or undefined. Property names and strings use double quotes. JSON is commonly used in API payloads and configuration, but it is data—not a validation guarantee.
understand.whyItMatters: A predictable data format makes it easier for different programs and languages to exchange structured information.
understand.analogy: Think of a delivery process with a sender, a message, and a receiver who returns a confirmation or explanation.
understand.analogyLimit: Software communication may involve complex protocols, asynchronous timing, security, and partial failures that this everyday analogy cannot fully capture.

explain.narrative:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for representing structured data. It supports objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. JSON does not directly support comments, functions, or undefined. Property names and strings use double quotes. JSON is commonly used in API payloads and configuration, but it is data—not a validation guarantee.

Use the protocol and service documentation as the authoritative guide for a real API. Examples here are conceptual and intentionally do not make live network calls.

examples.title: Represent an object
examples.explanation: The text parses into a structured object.

examples.title: Use numeric data
examples.explanation: Parsed numbers can be used as numbers.

examples.title: Read a boolean
examples.explanation: JSON represents boolean values as true or false.

examples.title: Represent missing value as null
examples.explanation: JSON null is an explicit null value, not the same as an absent property.

commonMistakes: Assuming every request succeeds or returns the same shape.
Treating parsing as validation or authentication as authorization.
Ignoring timeout, rate-limit, and failure responses.
Embedding secret credentials in public client code.
Retrying operations without considering duplicate side effects.

guidedTask.instructions: Create a JSON object representing a course with title, lesson count, tags array, and published boolean. Parse it and access two fields.

independentTask.title: Independent Practice
independentTask.instructions: Design a JSON payload for a learner profile's public preferences. Include nested objects and arrays, omit private data, then check that it is valid JSON and explain each field.
requirements: Use a fictional or toy service; do not include live secrets.

hints: Use double quotes for strings and property names.
JSON does not allow comments or trailing commas.
Parsing does not validate business rules or permissions.

questions.prompt: Which data structures does JSON support?
options: Objects and arrays plus scalar values
questions.answer: Objects and arrays plus scalar values
questions.explanation: JSON is a data representation format.

questions.prompt: How must JSON string values be quoted?
questions.explanation: JSON string syntax requires double quotes.

questions.prompt: Which value is valid JSON boolean?
questions.explanation: JSON uses lowercase true and false.

questions.prompt: Can JSON contain a function value?
options: No; JSON represents data, not functions
questions.answer: No; JSON represents data, not functions
questions.explanation: Functions are not part of JSON's value types.

questions.prompt: Does successful JSON parsing prove data is acceptable to an application?
options: No; it still needs validation and relevant checks
Only if it contains an object
questions.answer: No; it still needs validation and relevant checks
questions.explanation: Parsing checks syntax, not application rules.
